facts.statement: The hoopoe starling lived on the island of Réunion and became extinct in the 1850s.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling (Fregilupus varius), also known as the Réunion starling or the Bourbon crested starling, is a species of starling that lived on the Mascarene island of Réunion and became extinct in the 1850s.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling had plumage that was primarily white and grey, with darker brown and grey on its back, wings, and tail.
facts.quote: Its plumage was primarily white and grey, with its back, wings and tail a darker brown and grey.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling had a light, mobile crest that curled forwards.
facts.quote: It had a light, mobile crest, which curled forwards.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the hoopoe starling was sexually dimorphic, with males being larger and having more curved beaks.
facts.quote: The bird is thought to have been sexually dimorphic, with males larger and having more curved beaks.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling reportedly lived in large flocks and inhabited humid areas and marshes.
facts.quote: Reportedly living in large flocks, it inhabited humid areas and marshes.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling's robust pelvis, large feet and claws, and strong jaws indicate it foraged near the ground.
facts.quote: Its pelvis was robust, its feet and claws large, and its jaws strong, indicating that it foraged near the ground.

facts.statement: In 1831, French naturalist René-Primevère Lesson placed the hoopoe starling in its own monotypic genus, Fregilipus.
facts.quote: In 1831, French naturalist René-Primevère Lesson placed the bird in its own monotypic genus, Fregilipus

facts.statement: German ornithologist Hermann Schlegel proposed in 1857 that the hoopoe starling belonged to the starling family and reclassified it as Sturnus capensis.
facts.quote: German ornithologist Hermann Schlegel first proposed in 1857 that the species belonged to the starling family, (Sturnidae), reclassifying it as part of the genus Sturnus, S. capensis.

facts.statement: Swedish zoologist Carl Jakob Sundevall proposed the genus name Lophopsarus in 1872, but Fregilupus varius remains the valid binomial name as it is the oldest.
facts.quote: Swedish zoologist Carl Jakob Sundevall proposed the new genus name Lophopsarus ("crested starling") in 1872, yet Fregilupus varius—the oldest name—remains the bird's binomial, and all other scientific names are synonyms.

facts.statement: British zoologist James Murie agreed in 1874 that the hoopoe starling was a starling after analyzing its skeleton.
facts.quote: In 1874, after a detailed analysis of the only known skeleton (held at the Cambridge University Museum of Zoology), British zoologist James Murie agreed that it was a starling.

facts.statement: American ornithologist Andrew John Berger cast doubt on the hoopoe starling's relationship with starlings in 1957 due to subtle anatomical differences.
facts.quote: In 1957, American ornithologist Andrew John Berger cast doubt on the bird's affinity with starlings because of subtle anatomical differences, after dissecting a spirit specimen at the American Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: Some authors proposed a relationship between the hoopoe starling and vangas, but this was rejected by Japanese ornithologist Hiroyuki Morioka in 1996.
facts.quote: Some authors proposed a relationship with vangas (Vangidae), but Japanese ornithologist Hiroyuki Morioka rejected this in 1996, after a comparative study of skulls.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling's lineage diverged from other starlings 4 million years ago, suggesting it may have first evolved on now-submerged landmasses.
facts.quote: Its lineage diverged from that of other starlings 4 million years ago (about 2 million years before Réunion emerged from the sea), so it may have first evolved on landmasses now partially submerged.

facts.statement: The divergence of the hoopoe starling's lineage converged with the emergence of Réunion between 2.1 and 3.0 million years ago, without evidence of stepping-stone dispersal.
facts.quote: Their divergence estimate converged with the emergence of Réunion 2.1–3.0 million years ago, and did not indicate stepping stone dispersal.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest a sea-level increase during the last interglacial period may have reduced the hoopoe starling's habitat and caused a population decrease.
facts.quote: The decrease in its population was perhaps due to a sea-level increase caused by the last interglacial period, which reduced the bird's habitat on the island.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling was the largest of the three Mascarene starlings.
facts.quote: It was the largest of the three Mascarene starlings.

facts.statement: The bird has an ash-brown back and tail, darker wings with a greyish wash, and upper tail coverts and rump with a rufous wash.
facts.quote: Its back and tail are ash-brown, its wings darker with a greyish wash, and its upper tail covert feathers and rump have a rufous wash.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling had lemon-yellow beaks and legs with yellow-brown claws.
facts.quote: The beak and legs are lemon-yellow, with yellow-brown claws.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the type illustration of the hoopoe starling was a life drawing or a derivative of an earlier drawing by Jossigny.
facts.quote: Hume believes that Martinet did this when he made the type illustration, and it was derivative of Jossigny's image rather than a life drawing.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling was an omnivore that fed on fruits, seeds, and insects.
facts.quote: Like most other starlings, the hoopoe starling was omnivorous, feeding on fruits, seeds, and insects.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling had robust pelvic elements and large feet and claws, suggesting it foraged near the ground.
facts.quote: Its pelvic elements were robust and its feet and claws large, indicating that it foraged near the ground.

facts.statement: A dissected specimen's stomach contents included seeds and berries of Pseudobuxus, possibly Eugenia buxifolia.
facts.quote: De Montbeillard was informed of the stomach contents of a dissected specimen, consisting of seeds and the berries of "Pseudobuxus" (possibly Eugenia buxifolia, a bush with sweet, orange berries).

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling likely nested in tree cavities.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling probably nested in tree cavities.

facts.statement: In 2020, researchers noted the hoopoe starling had black skin and light plumage, which may have evolved to protect against ultraviolet radiation.
facts.quote: Belgian biologist Michaël P. J. Nicolaï and colleagues pointed out in 2020 that the hoopoe starling had black skin combined with light plumage and lived in high irradiation zones, which may have evolved for protection against ultraviolet irradiation in this and other black-skinned birds.

facts.statement: Two specimens from the aviary of Julien Desjardins were sent to the Paris museum in 1839.
facts.quote: Two specimens that had lived in the aviary of French natural historian Julien Desjardins were pickled and given to the Paris museum in 1839.

facts.statement: The last definite record of a live hoopoe starling was taken in 1836.
facts.quote: The final specimen on the island (the last definite record of a live specimen anywhere) was taken in 1836.

facts.statement: The only known subfossil specimen is a femur discovered in 1993 in a Réunion grotto.
facts.quote: The only known subfossil hoopoe starling specimen is a femur, discovered in 1993 in a Réunion grotto.

facts.statement: It is suggested that the introduction of the common myna led to competition with the hoopoe starling.
facts.quote: An oft-repeated suggestion is that the introduction of the common myna (Acridotheres tristis) led to competition between these two starling species.

facts.statement: Hume argued that over-hunting by a growing human population was the final blow that drove the species to extinction.
facts.quote: According to Hume, over-hunting was the final blow to the species; with forests more accessible, hunting by the rapidly growing human population may have driven the remaining birds to extinction.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling was the last of the Mascarene starling species to go extinct.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling survived longer than many other extinct Mascarene species, and was the last of the Mascarene starling species to face extinction.

facts.statement: Fregilupus varius, known as the Réunion crested starling, is an extinct passerine bird from the family Sturnidae that was endemic to Réunion in the Mascarene Islands.
facts.quote: El estornino de Reunión o estornino crestado de Reunión (Fregilupus varius) es una especie extinta de ave paseriforme de la familia Sturnidae endémica de Reunión, en las islas Mascareñas.

facts.statement: The bird measured approximately 30 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: Medía unos 30 centímetros de longitud.

facts.statement: Its plumage was mostly white and gray, with the back, wings, and tail being dark brown and gray.
facts.quote: Su plumaje era sobre todo de color blanco y gris, con la parte posterior, las alas y la cola de un color marrón oscuro y gris.

facts.statement: It possessed a slight erect crest that curved forward.
facts.quote: Tenía una ligera cresta eréctil, que se curvaba hacia delante.

facts.statement: Researchers believe the species exhibited sexual dimorphism, with males being larger and having a more curved bill than females.
facts.quote: Se cree que la especie poseía cierto dimorfismo sexual, siendo los machos más grandes y con el pico más curvo que las hembras.

facts.statement: Reports indicate the birds lived in large flocks and inhabited wetlands and marshes.
facts.quote: Según los informes vivían en grandes bandadas y habitaba en zonas húmedas y pantanos.

facts.statement: The species was omnivorous, feeding on plant matter and insects.
facts.quote: Era omnívoro, se alimentan de materia vegetal y de insectos.

facts.statement: Its robust pelvis, long toes with large claws, and strong jaws suggest it foraged for food near the ground.
facts.quote: Su pelvis era robusta, tenía dedos largos con garras grandes y mandíbulas fuertes lo que indica que buscaba alimento cerca del suelo.

facts.statement: Only nineteen specimens of the species are preserved worldwide.
facts.quote: Se conservan solo diecinueve especímenes en todo el mundo.

facts.statement: The first mention of the bird is believed to be in a 1658 list of birds from Madagascar written by French governor Étienne de Flacourt.
facts.quote: Se cree que la primera vez donde aparece mencionado el estornino crestado de Reunión es en una lista de aves de Madagascar de 1658 escrita por el gobernador francés Étienne de Flacourt.

facts.statement: The bird was first recorded on the island of Réunion (then called Bourbon) by Père Vachet in 1669, but was not described in detail until Sieur Dubois's report in 1674.
facts.quote: El estornino crestado fue registrado por primera vez en la isla de Reunión (entonces llamada "Bourbon") por Père Vachet en 1669, pero no fue descrito en detalle hasta el informe de Sieur Dubois de 1674

facts.statement: Although scientifically described by French naturalist Philippe Guéneau de Montbeillard in the 1779 edition of Buffon's Histoire Naturelle, it did not receive its scientific name until Dutch naturalist Pieter Boddaert assigned it in the 1783 edition.
facts.quote: Aunque la especie fue descrita científicamente por el naturalista francés Philippe Guéneau de Montbeillard en la edición de 1779 de la Histoire Naturelle del conde de Buffon, no recibió su nombre científico hasta que se lo asignó el naturalista holandés Pieter Boddaert en la edición de la obra de 1783.

facts.statement: Boddaert named it Upupa varia, classifying it in the hoopoe genus, meaning "mottled hoopoe" in reference to its white and dark colors.
facts.quote: Boddaert lo denominó Upupa varia, clasificándolo en el género de las abubillas, por lo que su nombre científico significaba «abubilla abigarrada», en referencia a sus colores blanco y oscuro.

facts.statement: In 1831, René-Primevère Lesson placed it in its own genus, Fregilipus, a combination of Upupa and Fregilus, the latter being an obsolete name for coucals.
facts.quote: En 1831, René-Primevère Lesson lo situó en su propio género, Fregilipus, una combinación de Upupa y Fregilus, este último el nombre de un género obsoleto usado para las chovas.

facts.statement: Hermann Schlegel first proposed in 1857 that the species belonged to the starling family (Sturnidae), reclassifying it within the genus Sturnus as S. capensis.
facts.quote: Hermann Schlegel propuso por primera vez en 1857 que la especie pertenecía a la familia de los estorninos (Sturnidae), reclasificándolo dentro del género Sturnus como S. capensis.

facts.statement: Carl Jakob Sundevall proposed the genus name Lophopsarus in 1872, but Fregilupus varius remains the valid binomial name, with all others being synonyms.
facts.quote: Carl Jakob Sundevall propuso un nuevo nombre para su propio género Lophopsarus (estornino crestado) en 1872, aunque Fregilupus varius—el nombre correcto más antiguo—prevalece como nombre binomial del ave y todos los demás nombres científicos quedan como sinónimos.

facts.statement: In 1941, Malcolm R. Miller found the bird's musculature similar to the common starling after dissecting an alcohol-preserved specimen, but noted the degraded tissue did not necessarily confirm a relationship with starlings.
facts.quote: En 1941 Malcolm R. Miller encontró que la musculatura del ave era similar a la del estornino común (Sturnus vulgaris) tras diseccionar un espécimen conservado en alcohol en el museo de Cambridge, pero anotó que el tejido estaba muy degradado y que la similitud no confirmaba necesariamente una relación con los estorninos.

facts.statement: In 1957, Andrew John Berger doubted the bird's relationship with starlings due to subtle anatomical differences after dissecting another alcohol-preserved specimen at the American Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: En 1957 Andrew John Berger albergó dudas sobre el parentesco de esta ave con los estorninos debido a sutiles diferencias anatómicas, tras diseccionar otro espécimen conservado en alcohol en el Museo Americano de Historia Natural.

facts.statement: Other authors proposed a relationship with vangas (Vangidae), but Hiroyuki Morioka rejected this in 1996 following a comparative study of their skeletons.
facts.quote: Otros autores propusieron una relación con los vangas (Vangidae), pero Hiroyuki Morioka lo rechazo en 1996, tras un estudio comparativo de sus esqueletos.

facts.quote: Time range: Holocene to Holocene (0.0117 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: In 1875, Alfred Newton hypothesized that a black and white bird mentioned in a 1726–27 manuscript by a mariner stranded on Rodrigues was the same species as the Réunion crested starling.
facts.quote: En 1875 el ornitólogo británico Alfred Newton intentó identificar con el estornino de Reunión un pájaro blanco y negro mencionado en un manuscrito del que describía un marinero abandonado en las isla de Rodrigues (también de las Mascareñas) entre 1726–27, suponiendo que podría tratarse de la misma especie.

facts.statement: Although Günther and Newton found the Rodrigues bird closely related to the Réunion crested starling, they assigned them to separate genera.
facts.quote: Aunque encontraron que esta ave de Rodrigues estaba cercanamente emparentada con el estornino crestado de Reunión, Günther y Newton les asignaron géneros separados.

facts.statement: In 2014, Julian P. Hume described the extinct Mauritius starling (Cryptopsar ischyrhynchus) from subfossils, noting it was more closely related to the Rodrigues starling than to the Réunion crested starling based on skull, sternum, and humerus characteristics.
facts.quote: En 2014 el paleontólogo británico Julian P. Hume describió una nueva especie extinta: el estornino de Mauricio (Cryptopsar ischyrhynchus), a partir de subfósiles de Mauricio, que estaba más próximamente emparentada con el estornino de Rodrigues que el crestado de Reunión por las características de su cráneo, esternón y húmero.
